## One expression, two directions

Suppose a coin lands heads 7 times in 10 independent flips. The unknown probability of heads is \(p\). It is tempting to say, “the probability that \(p=0.7\) is largest.” That sentence quietly confuses **probability** with **likelihood**.

Probability reasons forward: if \(p\) were known, how probable would the data be? For \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\),

$$
\Pr(K=k\mid p)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
$$

Likelihood reverses what varies. After observing \(k\), the data are fixed and candidate values of \(p\) are compared:

$$
L(p\mid k,n)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad 0\le p\le 1.
$$

The formula is identical, but its role is different. As a function of \(k\), it is a probability distribution when \(p\) is fixed. As a function of \(p\), it is a likelihood when \(k\) is fixed. A likelihood need not sum or integrate to one over parameter values. Therefore, \(L(0.7)\) is not \(\Pr(p=0.7\mid K=7)\); a probability distribution for \(p\) requires additional assumptions, such as a Bayesian prior.

## Comparing candidate coins

Because likelihoods can be extremely small, it is useful to divide every value by the largest one. This creates a **relative likelihood** whose maximum is 1 without changing which \(p\) fits best.

```{r}
#| label: likelihood-data
#| tbl-cap: "Selected candidate values for the probability of heads."
n <- 10
k <- 7

candidate_p <- c(0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90)
candidate_loglik <- dbinom(k, size = n, prob = candidate_p, log = TRUE)
candidate_relative <- exp(candidate_loglik - max(candidate_loglik))

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Candidate p` = sprintf("%.2f", candidate_p),
  `Probability of exactly 7 heads` = sprintf("%.4f", exp(candidate_loglik)),
  `Relative likelihood` = sprintf("%.3f", candidate_relative),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

Among these candidates, \(p=0.7\) supports the observed result most strongly. A smooth curve shows that it is also the best value among all candidates between 0 and 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-likelihood
#| fig-cap: "Relative likelihood after observing 7 heads in 10 flips. The curve compares parameter values; it is not a probability density for p."
#| fig-alt: "A smooth likelihood curve reaches its maximum of one at p equals 0.7 and falls toward zero near p equals zero and one."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
p_grid <- seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 1000)
loglik_10 <- dbinom(k, size = n, prob = p_grid, log = TRUE)
relative_10 <- exp(loglik_10 - max(loglik_10))

local({
  old <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  on.exit(par(old))
  plot(p_grid, relative_10, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#246B8E",
       xlab = "Candidate probability of heads, p",
       ylab = "Relative likelihood", ylim = c(0, 1.04), las = 1)
  abline(v = k / n, lty = 2, col = "#C44E52")
  points(k / n, 1, pch = 19, col = "#C44E52")
  text(k / n, 0.91, expression(hat(p) == 0.7), pos = 4,
       col = "#C44E52")
})
```

## Why the maximum is the sample proportion

Products are easier to differentiate after taking logarithms. Since logarithms are strictly increasing, maximizing \(L\) is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood:

$$
\ell(p)=\log L(p)=\log\binom{n}{k}+k\log p+(n-k)\log(1-p).
$$

For (0<k<n), differentiate and set the score equal to zero:

$$
\ell'(p)=\frac{k}{p}-\frac{n-k}{1-p}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k(1-p)=(n-k)p
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat p=\frac{k}{n}.
$$

This stationary point is the unique maximum because

$$
\ell''(p)=-\frac{k}{p^2}-\frac{n-k}{(1-p)^2}<0
\qquad (0<p<1).
$$

Thus the entire log-likelihood is strictly concave. If \(k=0\) or \(k=n\), there is no interior stationary point; the maximum occurs at the boundary, \(\widehat p=0\) or \(1\). These cases matter because blindly solving a derivative equation would miss them.

## Same estimate, different evidence

Now compare 7 heads in 10 flips with 70 heads in 100 flips. Both give \(\widehat p=0.7\), but the larger experiment should tell us more. Its likelihood curve is much sharper.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sample-size
#| fig-cap: "Both samples have the same maximum-likelihood estimate, but 70 heads in 100 flips produces a more concentrated likelihood."
#| fig-alt: "Two relative-likelihood curves peak at 0.7. The curve for 70 heads out of 100 is considerably narrower than the curve for 7 out of 10."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
relative_likelihood <- function(p, successes, trials) {
  values <- dbinom(successes, size = trials, prob = p, log = TRUE)
  exp(values - max(values))
}

rel_10 <- relative_likelihood(p_grid, 7, 10)
rel_100 <- relative_likelihood(p_grid, 70, 100)

local({
  old <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1.2, 0.8))
  on.exit(par(old))
  plot(p_grid, rel_10, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#D07629",
       xlab = "Candidate probability of heads, p",
       ylab = "Relative likelihood", ylim = c(0, 1.04), las = 1)
  lines(p_grid, rel_100, lwd = 3, col = "#246B8E")
  abline(v = 0.7, lty = 3, col = "grey35")
  legend("topleft", c("7 heads / 10 flips", "70 heads / 100 flips"),
         col = c("#D07629", "#246B8E"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
})
```

The connection is mathematical. At the maximum,

$$
-\ell''(\widehat p)=\frac{n}{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}.
$$

Larger \(n\) creates greater curvature and a narrower peak. In regular large samples, the inverse curvature gives the approximation

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\widehat p)\approx
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{n}}.
$$

It equals about 0.145 for 7/10 and 0.046 for 70/100. This approximation can be poor for small samples or estimates near 0 or 1, so the shape of the likelihood remains informative.

```{r}
#| label: verification
#| include: false
p_hat <- k / n
score_at_mle <- k / p_hat - (n - k) / (1 - p_hat)
curvature <- -k / p_hat^2 - (n - k) / (1 - p_hat)^2
se_10 <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 10)
se_100 <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 100)

stopifnot(abs(score_at_mle) < 1e-12,
          curvature < 0,
          abs(p_grid[which.max(relative_10)] - p_hat) < 0.002,
          abs(max(relative_10) - 1) < 1e-12,
          abs(se_10 - 0.1449138) < 1e-6,
          abs(se_100 - 0.04582576) < 1e-6)
```

## Assumptions, source, and takeaway

The numbers are constructed for this explanation; no external dataset is used. The binomial model assumes a fixed number of independent flips with one constant \(p\). Dependence or a changing coin would require a different likelihood. R. A. Fisher’s [1922 paper on the foundations of theoretical statistics](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1922.0009) helped formalize likelihood as distinct from inverse probability.

::: {.callout-note title="Takeaway"}
Maximum likelihood ranks parameter values by how well they explain fixed, observed data. The maximizer \(\widehat p=k/n\) is a point estimate, not the probability that the parameter is correct. The peak’s width supplies the missing second lesson: two identical estimates can carry very different amounts of information.
:::
